Every story in this collection ends the same way:
something real appears.

Treasures That Teach is a bilingual app where children work through five true social–emotional stories — then the page turns, and a photograph of the real object behind the story is revealed. A carved stool. A cowrie–shell mask. A drum, a braid, a balafon. Not illustrations of culture — documentation of it.

Why a photograph

Representation is not a mood board. It is a specific object, a real people, a source you can name.

Most social–emotional apps illustrate a feeling and move on. Treasures That Teach does the slower, harder thing: it ties each feeling to a real object, researches that object properly, and only then lets a child meet it — honestly, at their level, in their own language.

01

Researched, not decorated

Every object's history is checked against real sources — museum records, academic Africanist scholarship, UNESCO documentation — before a single word reaches a child's screen. Claims that can't be sourced don't ship.

02

Bilingual by construction

Every line a child hears or reads exists natively in English and Latin American Spanish — not machine–translated, authored twice, in voice.

03

Built to be believed

Grown–ups get their own page after every story: what's confirmed, what the object's real cultural context is, and where the gallery's own research is still open.

“This is a real stool. Somebody carved every one of those birds, and every line on the seat above them, out of one piece of wood. It sits in a real collection today.”

— from the reveal page, Story One

The next chapter

Five objects are open. The gallery holds many more.

Treasures That Teach launched with five fully researched, fully bilingual stories — each one built the slow way, on purpose. Support at this stage goes directly into the parts of the work that don't shortcut: specialist review of objects still pending confirmation, new stories built around the rest of the Sanders–McCray Gallery, and getting this into more classrooms and more homes, in both languages, at no cost to the families who need it most.
